strengths: The paper addresses a significant and overlooked gap in shadow detection by explicitly separating and targeting attached shadows alongside cast shadows.
The proposed framework elegantly integrates physical principles (combining 3D surface normals and light direction) with deep learning in an iterative, closed-loop feedback design.
The curation and release of a new dataset of 1,458 images with explicit, manual annotations for both cast and attached shadows is a highly valuable contribution to the community.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate a substantial reduction in Balanced Error Rate (BER) for attached shadow detection while maintaining strong performance on cast shadows.
weaknesses: The light estimation performance is not quantitatively evaluated (e.g., using angular error) in the main paper, despite being a core component of the iterative framework.

The framework relies on several off-the-shelf components, such as Depth Anything v2 for normal estimation and BiRefNet for object masking, which makes the system sensitive to the failure modes of these external models.
The assumption of a single directional light source limits the applicability of the method in complex, multi-light indoor scenes.
The heuristic method used to estimate ground-truth 3D light directions for the SOBA and CUHK datasets might introduce noise during training.

strengths: Addresses an Underserved Problem: Most current deep learning research on shadow detection targets cast shadows. This work explicitly distinguishes and models attached shadows, which are crucial for 3D shape perception.

Physics-Grounded Closed-Loop Architecture: Combining deep segmentation networks with classical lighting and geometry equations ($n \cdot \ell > 0$) in an iterative closed-loop feedback design is technically sound, intuitive, and effective.

Valuable Dataset Contribution: Curating a dataset of 1,458 images with manual, separate annotations for cast and attached shadows is a significant contribution that can enable future research in this direction.

Strong Quantitative and Qualitative Results: The proposed method outperforms prior methods significantly in attached shadow detection (reducing the BER by over 33% relative to retrained baselines) while remaining highly competitive on cast shadows.
weaknesses: Lack of Quantitative Light Estimation Evaluation: While the light direction estimator is key to the feedback loop, there is no quantitative evaluation of the predicted 3D light directions (e.g., reporting angular error in degrees against the generated ground-truth light directions). This makes it hard to verify if the physical light estimation itself is accurate or just acts as a regularizer.

Simplifying Lighting Assumption: The assumption of a single global directional light source is highly restrictive. In many indoor and multi-source environments, the $n \cdot \ell > 0$ formulation will fail to accurately represent attached shadows.

Heavy Dependence on Monocular Normal Quality: As shown in the limitations, the method is highly sensitive to the quality of the relative depth/normals from Depth Anything V2. Since monocular normal estimation remains an open challenge, this introduces a critical external dependency.

Increased Computational Cost: Running the model iteratively (3 steps) increases the inference time from 0.18 seconds to 0.55 seconds, which represents a significant overhead for video processing or real-time applications.

strengths: Addresses an important yet under-explored problem in shadow detection: the explicit separation of cast and attached shadows.
Proposes an elegant, physics-grounded closed-loop framework that iteratively refines both shadow masks and 3D light direction using surface normals.
Curates and introduces a much-needed dataset of 1,458 images with separate manual annotations for cast and attached shadows, along with estimated 3D light directions.
Demonstrates significant quantitative improvements, reducing the Balanced Error Rate (BER) for attached shadows by at least 33% over retrained SOTA baselines.
weaknesses: Relies heavily on external monocular normal estimation (Depth Anything v2); errors in the normal maps directly impact the quality of the partial attached shadow maps.
The ground-truth 3D light directions for a large portion of the dataset (SOBA and CUHK) are derived from a simplified centroid-displacement heuristic, which might introduce noise during training.
The physical formulation assumes a single directional light source, limiting applicability to complex real-world environments with multi-source, diffuse, or omnidirectional lighting.
The iterative inference process increases computational overhead (around 3x compared to a single-pass model), which may limit real-time applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a novel and important task: joint detection of cast and attached shadows, which has been largely overlooked or treated uniformly by existing shadow detection methods.

The proposed iterative feedback loop between the shadow detection module and the light estimation module is physically grounded and elegant, successfully leveraging the reciprocal relationship between shadow formation and scene lighting.
The authors contribute a newly curated dataset of 1,458 images with high-quality, manually annotated cast and attached shadow masks, which will be highly valuable for the research community.

Strong quantitative and qualitative results are provided, showing a substantial 33% reduction in attached shadow BER compared to fine-tuned SOTA baselines, alongside demonstrating practical benefits in downstream shadow removal validated by a user study.
weaknesses: The framework heavily relies on the quality of estimated depth/normals from an off-the-shelf model (Depth-Anything-V2). As shown in the limitations section, errors in the geometry estimation directly propagate and cause incorrect shadow predictions.

The lighting formulation is simplified to a single dominant directional light source, which limits the model's applicability in complex scenes with multi-source, indoor, or highly diffuse/indirect illumination.

The iterative refinement scheme introduces noticeable computational overhead at inference time; the 3-step configuration is roughly 4 times slower than the non-iterative baseline, although it still remains within a practical range of ~0.55 seconds.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively under-explored task: jointly detecting and distinguishing cast and attached shadows, which are physically distinct and provide different cues for downstream applications.

A physically grounded, iterative refinement scheme is proposed, establishing a closed feedback loop between light direction estimation and shadow detection via intermediate geometry-derived partial attached shadow maps.
The authors introduce a newly curated dataset with manually corrected/annotated cast and attached shadow masks, which will be highly beneficial for future research in this direction.

Thorough experiments are presented, including quantitative and qualitative comparisons, extensive ablation studies, cross-dataset generalization evaluations, and a downstream application to shadow removal supported by a user study.
weaknesses: The framework relies heavily on external normal maps generated from depth estimation models (e.g., Depth-Anything-V2). Errors in geometry can propagate and corrupt the light reasoning loop, and the paper lacks a detailed quantitative sensitivity analysis on normal map quality.

The single scene-wide directional light assumption is quite simple and may fail under complex lighting conditions (such as multiple indoor lights, soft shadows from area lights, or heavy ambient/indirect lighting).

The iterative refinement mechanism introduces substantial computational overhead. The 3-iteration pipeline is about 3x to 4x slower than the non-iterative baseline, limiting its suitability for real-time applications.

In the experiments, the baselines are evaluated by using object masks to split their predicted joint masks. A fairer and stronger baseline comparison would involve retraining some of these SOTA models directly on the proposed multi-class {background, cast, attached} labels to see how well they perform when trained with the same supervision.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and under-explored task: explicitly distinguishing between cast and attached shadows, which has valuable downstream applications in 3D reconstruction and shadow removal.
The authors introduce a newly curated dataset of 1,458 images with manually annotated cast, attached, and undefined shadow masks, derived from three existing benchmarks.
The qualitative results demonstrate that separating cast and attached shadows can lead to more natural-looking shadow removal results by enabling targeted refinement.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons: The compared baselines are retrained using only binary full-shadow masks and then split post-hoc at test time using object masks to evaluate cast vs. attached performance. A fair comparison requires retraining these baseline networks (which is straightforward by changing the final layer's output channels) directly on the 3-class segmentation task (background, cast, attached) using the same supervision.

Mathematically flawed physical modeling: The surface normals are computed by taking spatial gradients of relative depth maps predicted by Depth-Anything-V2. Since monocular depth models predict relative depth up to an unknown scale and shift, taking their spatial gradients does not mathematically yield true physical surface normals. Using these inaccurate normals with a heuristic light direction in a physical dot product ($n \cdot \ell > 0$) is physically and mathematically inconsistent.

Non-differentiable feedback loop: The step to generate the partial attached shadow map (Equation 1) relies on a hard thresholding operation ($n \cdot \ell > 0$). This makes the feedback loop non-differentiable, meaning gradients cannot flow from the shadow detector back to the light estimator during joint training. This architectural limitation and its implications on training dynamics are not addressed.

Incomplete downstream evaluation: The shadow removal application is only evaluated qualitatively via a user study, with the authors claiming that their dataset lacks shadow-free ground truth. However, since the WSRD subset contains paired shadow and shadow-free images, a quantitative evaluation of shadow removal on this subset should have been conducted to substantiate the claims.
